items.title: Invasive species, drought threaten water on 3 continents

featured_image.name: 53 lakes dry up as city waits for monsoon relief

items.description: From dried-up lakes in southern India to a deepening water crisis across Türkiye and aging infrastructure in the U.S. Midwest, a convergence of invasive species, drought, and extreme weather is threatening water and food supplies across three continents. New research, government warnings, and expert testimony this week underscored the urgency of the challenges facing billions of people who depend on increasingly fragile water systems.

items.title: Flinders University scientists develop nano-cage that removes 98% of PFAS from water

featured_image.name: Nano-cage removes up to 98% of PFAS in tap water tests

items.description:
Researchers at Flinders University in South Australia have developed a nano-sized molecular cage that can remove more than 98 percent of toxic "forever chemicals" from tap water, offering a potential breakthrough in tackling one of the most persistent forms of water contamination worldwide.

The study, published in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition, details how the team led by Dr. Witold Bloch engineered a molecular cage that acts as a highly selective trap for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS. The method is notable for its ability to capture short-chain PFAS — smaller, more water-soluble variants that have long eluded conventional water treatment technologies.[1][2][3]

items.title: Ivory Coast to slash cocoa farmer prices in historic move

featured_image.name: Ivory Coast to announce cocoa mid-crop price by end of month ...

items.description:
Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, will bring forward the start of its cocoa mid-crop season for the first time in history and sharply reduce prices paid to farmers, according to two government sources and two regulatory sources who spoke to Reuters. The move is designed to help the West African nation clear a growing pile of unsold cocoa that has accumulated at ports and inland storage sites in recent months.[1]

Under the plan, cocoa harvested beginning in March will be classified as mid-crop rather than main crop, with the farmer price set at between 800 and 1,000 CFA francs ($1.45 to $1.81) per kilogram — a steep drop from the current main crop rate of 2,800 CFA francs. The mid-crop traditionally begins in April and runs through September, but it will now start on March 1 and end a month earlier, in late August. The changes were approved by an interministerial committee overseeing raw materials last week.[2][3][1]

items.title: Rutgers study challenges theory that melting glaciers could slow climate change

featured_image.name: Antarctica's ice shelves could be melting faster than we thought

items.description:
Marine scientists at Rutgers University have found that meltwater from an Antarctic ice shelf delivers far less iron to the surrounding ocean than long assumed, upending a widely held theory that glacier-driven iron fertilization could act as a natural brake on climate change. The findings were published Tuesday in the journal Communications Earth and Environment.[1]

The theory posits that as rising temperatures cause Antarctic glaciers to melt, the iron released would nourish blooms of microscopic algae in the Southern Ocean. Those algae absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, theoretically pulling heat-trapping gas from the atmosphere. But direct sampling beneath the Dotson Ice Shelf in West Antarctica's Amundsen Sea has shown the mechanism is far weaker than models predicted.[2]

items.title: Oil holds near 7-month highs as US-Iran talks open in Geneva

featured_image.name: US-Iran talks live: Nuclear talks to kick off in Geneva amid ...

items.description:
Oil prices edged higher on Thursday, hovering near seven-month highs, as investors weighed whether a third round of nuclear talks between the United States and Iran could avert a military confrontation that threatens to disrupt crude supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures traded near $71 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate held around $65.50, both largely flat after settling with minimal changes on Wednesday, according to Reuters. Brent had earlier in the week reached its highest level since late July as Washington continued to position military forces in the region to pressure Tehran into a deal.[1]

items.title: Scripps Research finds hidden structure in cell droplets, opening new drug targets

featured_image.name: What rules govern the structure of membraneless organelles?

items.description: Scientists at Scripps Research have upended a long-standing assumption in cell biology by discovering that some biomolecular condensates — the membrane-less, droplet-like compartments that cells use to organize essential processes — contain intricate internal networks of protein filaments. The findings, published in Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, point to new therapeutic possibilities for diseases including cancer and neurodegeneration.[1][2]

items.title: UN issues first carbon credits under Paris Agreement

featured_image.name: UN's new carbon market delivers first credits

items.description:
The United Nations on Thursday approved the first-ever carbon credits under the global carbon market established by the Paris Agreement, a milestone for international climate finance that has been more than a decade in the making — and one that has already drawn scrutiny from environmental watchdogs.

The approved credits stem from a clean-cooking project in Myanmar that distributes efficient wood-burning cookstoves to reduce household air pollution and ease pressure on local forests, the UNFCCC announced in a press release. The project, coordinated with a South Korean company, will generate credits counting toward the climate targets of both South Korea and Myanmar.[1][2]

items.title: Nvidia's record Q4 earnings send Asian markets to new highs

featured_image.name: Nvidia beats on Q4 expectations and offers better-than ...

items.description:
Asian stock markets rallied on Thursday after Nvidia reported record fourth-quarter revenue that handily topped Wall Street forecasts, easing concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom. US and European futures, however, drifted lower as investors weighed the chipmaker's results alongside lingering trade-policy uncertainty.

Nvidia posted quarterly revenue of $68.1 billion for the three months ending January 25, a 73% jump from the year-ago period and roughly $2 billion above analysts' consensus estimates. Non-GAAP earnings per share came in at $1.62, beating expectations of around $1.53. The company also guided for $78 billion in first-quarter revenue, well ahead of the approximately $72 billion Wall Street had penciled in.[1][2][3][4]

"Computing demand is growing exponentially — the agentic AI inflection point has arrived," CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement, adding that customers "are racing to invest in AI compute". On the earnings call, Huang declared that "AI is here, AI is not going to go back".[5][2]

items.title: Tropical flowers blooming weeks later due to climate change, study finds

featured_image.name: Tropical flowers are blooming weeks later than they used to ...

items.description:
Tropical plants are flowering weeks or even months earlier or later than they once did as a result of climate change, according to a study of more than 8,000 plant specimens collected over two centuries. The findings, published on February 25, 2026 in the journal PLOS One, challenge the long-held assumption that tropical ecosystems — home to more than half the world's plant biodiversity — are insulated from the phenological disruptions already documented in temperate and boreal regions.[1][2]

Researchers Skylar Graves and Erin Manzitto-Tripp of the University of Colorado-Boulder analyzed museum herbarium specimens representing 33 tropical species with distinct annual flowering periods, collected between 1794 and 2024 from sites in Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, Ghana, Guinea, Thailand, and Bolivia. They found that flowering periods have shifted by an average of about two days per decade.[2][1]

items.title: Canada, South Korea sign military intel-sharing pact

featured_image.name: Canada and South Korea sign a defence agreement | CBC News

items.description:
Canada and South Korea signed a defense agreement on Wednesday focused on the exchange and protection of classified military information, as Ottawa looks to deepen ties with like-minded middle powers and Seoul positions itself to win a multibillion-dollar Canadian submarine contract.

The signing took place during the second Canada-Republic of Korea Foreign and Defence (2+2) Ministerial Meeting in Ottawa, where Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with their South Korean counterparts, Defence Minister Ahn Gyuback and Foreign Minister Cho Hyun.[1][2]
